## 1) Chart type
- **Top:** Pictogram / icon-based ranked grid of teams, with repeated sandwich icons representing quantity.
- **Bottom:** **Scatter plot**.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Top:** Uses a **small-multiples/grid layout** of team panels. No stacking in the chart sense; quantity is shown by repeated icons within each panel.
- **Bottom:** Single-panel scatter plot with points positioned by two quantitative axes. No faceting or stacking.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| NFL team (abbreviation/logo) | Categorical/nominal | Small-multiple panel identity; team logo/image; text label |
| Weekly Uncrustables consumed | Quantitative | Text value in each team panel; repeated sandwich icons/area/count in top panel; x-axis position in scatter plot |
| NFL standings (win-loss-tie percentage) | Quantitative | y-axis position in scatter plot |
| Sandwich unit key (“= 10”) | Quantitative scale annotation | Legend/key using one sandwich icon plus label |

image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Top:** Pictogram / icon-based ranked grid of teams, with repeated sandwich icons representing quantity.
- **Bottom:** **Scatter plot**.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Top:** Uses a **small-multiples/grid layout** of team panels. No stacking in the chart sense; quantity is shown by repeated icons within each panel.
- **Bottom:** Single-panel scatter plot with points positioned by two quantitative axes. No faceting or stacking.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| NFL team (abbreviation/logo) | Categorical/nominal | Small-multiple panel identity; team logo/image; text label |
| Weekly Uncrustables consumed | Quantitative | Text value in each team panel; repeated sandwich icons/area/count in top panel; x-axis position in scatter plot |
| NFL standings (win-loss-tie percentage) | Quantitative | y-axis position in scatter plot |
| Sandwich unit key (“= 10”) | Quantitative scale annotation | Legend/key using one sandwich icon plus label |

## 1) Chart type

- **Bottom:** Single-panel scatter plot with points positioned by two quantitative axes. No faceting or stacking.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

| Weekly Uncrustables consumed | Quantitative | Text value in each team panel; repeated sandwich icons/area/count in top panel; x-axis position in scatter plot |
| NFL standings (win-loss-tie percentage) | Quantitative | y-axis position in scatter plot |
| Sandwich unit key (“= 10”) | Quantitative scale annotation | Legend/key using one sandwich icon plus label |

## 1) Chart type
- **Top:** Pictogram / icon-based ranked grid of teams, with repeated sandwich icons representing quantity.
- **Bottom:** **Scatter plot**.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Top:** Uses a **small-multiples/grid layout** of team panels. No stacking in the chart sense; quantity is shown by repeated icons within each panel.
- **Bottom:** Single-panel scatter plot with points positioned by two quantitative axes. No faceting or stacking.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| NFL team (abbreviation/logo) | Categorical/nominal | Small-multiple panel identity; team logo/image; text label |
| Weekly Uncrustables consumed | Quantitative | Text value in each team panel; repeated sandwich icons/area/count in top panel; x-axis position in scatter plot |
| NFL standings (win-loss-tie percentage) | Quantitative | y-axis position in scatter plot |
| Sandwich unit key (“= 10”) | Quantitative scale annotation | Legend/key using one sandwich icon plus label |
raw_comment: There seems to be a weak positive relationship between the percentage of Uncrustables consumption and win loss percentage. Since this seems like an observational study, it isn't possible to prove whether or not eating Uncrustables directly led to a higher win percentage. Uncrustables seem to be somewhat dense in calories consider it is made with peanut butter and other calorie dense foods. Also, NFL teams with more players on the field - which may be due to frequent substitutions - will therefore lead to more Uncrustables being consumed. Taking in this information, it seems as if some winning teams just so happen to eat Uncrustables due to potential factors like these. This makes me wonder why some NFL teams decided to start consuming Uncrustables, and I would like to see whether or not the players themselves believe the Uncrustables are helping them. This may relate to my community as Uncrustables may elevate energy levels of my schools football team compared to other mid-break snacks, so it should be looked into. A catchy headline would be "Are Uncrustables affecting NFL win percentages?"

raw_comment:
Headline- Uncrustables: The Real MVP of the NFL
This graph illustrates the weekly Uncrustable consumption across NFL teams, with each Uncrustable displayed representing 10 actual sandwiches. I notice that the Denver Broncos consume the most, at 700 per week, while the Saints and Bengals consume the least, at 50 per week. Most teams seem to fall somewhere between 100 and 300 Uncrustables per week. Looking at the second graph, I notice that there’s no clear relationship between the number of Uncrustables eaten and a team’s win-loss percentage. However, teams consuming around 100 Uncrustables seem to land somewhere around 50%. 
I wonder why the Broncos eat so many Uncrustables? Are they handed out on the sidelines of practices and games, or are they just the team's favorite snack?  I also wonder if the winning or losses really have anything to do with the amount of Uncrustables they eat. 
This relates to me and my community because I play a sport at my high school. We are always getting snacks such as chips and oranges to get our energy up at half-time. It’s interesting to think about how food can play a role in both professional and school-level sports. It makes me wonder if we ate Uncrustables, we would win more.

This graph shows the tie between Uncrustable intake and NFL teams. I noticed that there is not necessarily a correlation between a high/low consumption rate and a higher/lower win rate. I also wonder when exactly these started becoming common in the NFL. Was it in the last decade, or has it been a longer tradition? Finally, I'm curious when these players are eating them. Is it during a game, post-game, throughout practice, etc? This applies to my community because I am an athlete, and we usually eat before practice(a quick snack), and this makes me curious if I should replace that snack with an Uncrustable(is there a benefit in doing so?).

This graph showcases the weekly consumption of Uncrustables across the NFL teams in the 2023 season.  The first thing I noticed was the number of Uncrustables consumed by the Denver Broncos, at 700 per week, which was over double the number of Uncrustables consumed by the Seattle Seahawks, at 320 per week.  I wonder why the Broncos have consumed a far greater amount than the rest of the teams.  I also noticed that the Bengals and the Saints consumed 50 Uncrustables per week, in last place.  I also noticed that the Denver Broncos' win-loss-tie percentage is around 50%, while many teams that consume less Uncrustables weekly have higher win-loss-tie percentages.  I wonder why exactly Uncrustables became the new halftime snack for the NFL, and why the Denver Broncos consume so many of them weekly.  I also wonder if the number of Uncrustables consumed truly affects the NFL teams' win-loss-tie percentage.  This relates to me and my community because my family and I are football fans, and it is interesting to see an unusual statistic about Uncrustables in the NFL.

raw_comment:
I notice that while the Denver Broncos consume the most Uncrustables—700 per week—their win percentage doesn’t seem to correlate with this high snack intake. In fact, teams with win rates above 70% typically eat fewer than 200 Uncrustables per week, showing little connection between snack consumption and performance. Many lower-performing teams (with win rates under 40%) also consume fewer Uncrustables, with Denver being the main outlier. This suggests that Uncrustables may be more tied to team culture or logistics rather than directly influencing a team’s success. I wonder why these teams prefer Uncrustables, and what led to the shift from the traditional halftime snack of oranges to something like Uncrustables. I also wonder what other factors, such as practice routines or team dynamics, contribute to a team’s win percentage, aside from snacks. Given the size and physical demands of football players, I also wonder how many Uncrustables each player consumes—since they likely need more than just one or two to feel full. This relates to my community and me because in local teams and sports, everyone has a game-time snack, but that doesn’t necessarily correlate with success. For example, on my high school soccer team, we had Gatorade and chips at halftime, but we rarely won. This shows that snacks, while important, might not be the key factor in determining performance.

Catchy headline: "Uncrustables and NFL Wins: Do Snacks Really Shape Success?"

| Sandwich unit key (“= 10”) | Quantitative scale annotation | Legend/key using one sandwich icon plus label |
raw_comment: The first graph depicts how many uncrustables the 24 shown teams eat each week. I noticed in the second graph that the number of uncrustables eaten by a team does not increase their standings or help them win more. I wonder why uncrustables are so popular for these teams to eat during halftime. Does the jelly give the players energy or is it just because the snack is easy and quick to eat? I also wonder how many uncrustables each player would eat considering football players are very muscular and physically big. DEN has the highest amount of weekly Uncrustables eaten, followed by SEA & JAX. Graph #2 shows the No. of Uncrustables eaten per week and the win-loss-tie % in NFL standings. Eating Uncrustables could also be seen as a fun little tradition within schools across the state.
